description: How the Depression, SA violence and elite scheming destroyed German democracy by 1933.
content_html:
The Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression in Germany

On 24 October 1929, the New York Stock Exchange collapsed. American banks immediately recalled the short-term loans that had underpinned Germany’s recovery since 1924. German factories lost their credit, banks failed, and unemployment rocketed. By the winter of 1932, over six million Germans were officially unemployed — approximately one in three workers. Millions more were on short-time working. The social consequences were devastating: hunger, poverty, family breakdown, and a pervasive sense of hopelessness.

Key Fact

In the 1928 Reichstag election, the Nazi Party won just 2.6% of the vote. By July 1932, at the height of the Depression, they won 37.4% — becoming the largest party in the Reichstag, though still without a majority.

The Political Impact of the Depression

Chancellor Heinrich Brüning responded to the Depression with austerity: he cut wages, benefits and public spending, using Article 48 emergency decrees because he could not get his budget through the Reichstag. His measures deepened the depression rather than ending it. The human cost of austerity, combined with mass unemployment, turned millions of voters towards the political extremes. The Communist Party (KPD) grew significantly, but the Nazis grew far faster.

Hitler’s electoral appeal was remarkable in its breadth. He promised different things to different groups: jobs and economic recovery to the unemployed; protection of property and anti-communism to the middle classes and farmers; national greatness and revenge for Versailles to nationalists; strong leadership to those who saw coalition governments as weak and ineffectual. His speeches were emotionally charged, exploiting fear and resentment with extraordinary skill. The Nazi Party built a sophisticated propaganda machine, using modern techniques including radio, cinema and mass rallies.

The SA (Sturmabteilung), known as the Brownshirts, played a dual role. Their street violence — brawls with communists, attacks on Jewish businesses, disruption of opposition meetings — created an atmosphere of chaos. But paradoxically, this chaos helped the Nazis: voters who feared disorder were told that only Hitler could restore order. The SA also provided a sense of belonging and purpose to unemployed young men who had nothing else. By 1932, the SA had around 400,000 members.

Political violence escalated dramatically in 1932. In the summer of that year, there were hundreds of political killings on the streets of Germany. The Weimar Republic seemed unable to protect its citizens. This apparent weakness further discredited democratic government and pushed more voters towards parties that promised decisive action.

Elite Scheming: Papen, Hindenburg and Schleicher

By 1932, the Weimar political system was effectively deadlocked. The Nazis were the largest party but had no majority. The communists were strong. Moderate parties were weak. President Paul von Hindenburg, an elderly field marshal who privately despised Hitler, refused to appoint him Chancellor. Instead, he appointed Franz von Papen, a conservative aristocrat, in June 1932.

Key Fact

Franz von Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler as Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Papen believed he could control Hitler by surrounding him with conservative ministers. He was fatally wrong — within eighteen months Hitler had dismantled the entire constitutional order.

Historians have debated whether Hitler’s appointment was primarily the result of mass popular support or elite political miscalculation. Both factors mattered. The Nazis had the largest share of the popular vote (37.4% in July 1932, falling to 33.1% in November 1932 — a sign that support may have peaked). But Hitler became Chancellor not through a majority election victory but through the behind-the-scenes deal-making of Papen and Hindenburg. Papen calculated that he could use Hitler’s mass support while keeping real power in conservative hands. General Kurt von Schleicher, who briefly replaced Papen as Chancellor in December 1932, lost Hindenburg’s support and resigned in January 1933.

On 30 January 1933, Adolf Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany. The decision was made not by the German people through the ballot box but by an ageing president and a scheming ex-chancellor who fatally underestimated the man they thought they could control.

It is worth noting that Hitler never won a majority of the vote in a free election. The Nazis peaked at 37.4% in July 1932 and fell back to 33.1% in November 1932 as the worst of the Depression eased slightly and some voters returned to moderate parties. Had Hindenburg appointed a different Chancellor and stabilised the political situation, the Nazi surge might have continued to decline. The tragedy of January 1933 was that democracy was not overthrown from below by an unstoppable popular revolution — it was surrendered from above by conservative elites who calculated they had more to fear from communism than from Hitler, and who believed their money, institutions and social position would protect them once they had put him in office. They were catastrophically wrong on every count.
exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark ‘How far do you agree’ essay on why Hitler became Chancellor, you must cover multiple factors — the Depression’s impact on voters, Hitler’s electoral appeal, the role of the SA, and the elite scheming of Papen and Hindenburg. The top band requires a substantiated overall judgement: which factor was most important, and why? Avoid simply listing factors one by one — weigh them against each other in your conclusion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash (1929) ended US loans, collapsed the German economy, and drove unemployment above six million by 1932, destroying faith in the Weimar Republic among millions of voters.
  • Nazi support surged from 2.6% (1928) to 37.4% (July 1932) as Hitler exploited fear, resentment and the appeal of strong leadership; the SA created violence that paradoxically boosted Nazi support.
  • Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 not through a majority election win but through the political miscalculation of Papen and Hindenburg, who believed they could control him.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the impact of the Great Depression on German society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific social impact with precise detail (e.g. by 1932 over six million officially unemployed; families unable to afford food; collapse of savings in bank failures). Secure (1–2): feature identified with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to poverty or unemployment. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hitler's electoral appeal between 1929 and 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. Hitler promised economic recovery and jobs to the unemployed; he offered anti-communism and protection of property to the middle classes and farmers; he exploited nationalist resentment of Versailles. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the rapid growth of the Nazi Party's electoral support between 1928 and 1932.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. the Great Depression caused mass unemployment and social despair, making voters receptive to radical promises; middle-class fear of communism drove voters to the Nazis as a bulwark against the KPD) with specific evidence and link to electoral growth. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed. Developing (2): cause stated briefly. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the role played by the SA in German politics between 1930 and 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. SA street violence created an atmosphere of instability that discredited the Weimar Republic's ability to maintain order; this paradoxically boosted Nazi support among voters who feared chaos; OR: the SA provided a movement for unemployed young men, turning personal desperation into political energy for the Nazis). Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the role played by Franz von Papen and President Hindenburg in Hitler's appointment as Chancellor.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler, believing he could control him; significance was it bypassed democratic process) AND over time (Papen's fatal miscalculation — Hitler destroyed the constitutional order within eighteen months). Secure (5–6): both time periods addressed. Developing (3–4): mainly descriptive. Emerging (1–2): brief mention without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'The Great Depression was the main reason why the Weimar Republic collapsed.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): sustained agreement (Depression caused mass unemployment, drove voters to extremes, paralysed Reichstag decision-making, brought existing structural weaknesses to a crisis point) AND disagreement (structural weaknesses pre-dated Depression — proportional representation, Article 48, hostile judiciary; elite scheming of Papen/Hindenburg; Hitler's own political skills and propaganda). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

flashcard_questions.a: The chaos they created made voters fear disorder and turn to the Nazis as the party of strong order.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Brüning and what was his response to the Depression?
flashcard_questions.a: Chancellor 1930–1932 who imposed austerity cuts using emergency decrees, deepening the crisis.
A conservative politician who persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler Chancellor, believing he could control him.

flashcard_questions.q: On what date was Hitler appointed Chancellor?

flashcard_questions.a: He believed conservative ministers surrounding Hitler could control him — Hitler dismantled democracy within 18 months.

glossary_terms.definition: German Chancellor 1930–1932 who attempted to cut public spending to balance the budget during the Depression, deepening the economic crisis.
The Sturmabteilung, or Stormtroopers — the Nazi Party's paramilitary wing, used to intimidate political opponents and create the impression that only the Nazis could restore order.
Germany's President from 1925, a conservative First World War field marshal who was deeply sceptical of the Weimar Republic and reluctant to appoint Hitler as Chancellor.
German Chancellor from December 1932 to January 1933; his failure to find a stable government led Papen and Hindenburg to turn to Hitler.
The global economic crisis triggered by the Wall Street Crash of October 1929, which caused mass unemployment in Germany and destabilised the Weimar Republic.
Conservative German politician who persuaded President Hindenburg to appoint Hitler as Chancellor in January 1933, fatally believing he could control him.
